title: Install a processor: lift the socket lever, open the shield, seat it on its keys, shut both
instruction: Install the processor in the empty socket. Pull the socket lever's handle up out from under its catch and lift the lever all the way open, then open the steel processor shield by its lip. Set the processor in the socket with its two notches on the socket's keys and its gold triangle at the socket's gold mark. Then shut the shield and press the lever back down under its catch.
context: Server technicians install a processor this way. Dell's PowerEdge R260 (an LGA1700 server) service video: "To install the processor, align and place the processor in the socket", then "Lower the processor shield, then lower the lever and push it under the tab to lock it into place." HPE's DL360 Gen9 guide warns that "Forcing the levers closed can damage the processor and socket, requiring system board replacement", and that the board's pins are very fragile. Done by: server and data-center technicians.
setup: Positions in cm on the table, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. A green server board 13 by 10 cm, 4 mm thick, fixed flat, from x 28 to 41, centred at y -11. On it, a processor socket centred at x 34, y -11: a pocket 45.5 by 38 mm (long side along x) inside a black frame 4 mm thick and 3.5 mm tall, whose two long walls have a 30 mm gap in the middle for fingers and whose inner top edges are rounded (1 mm); two gold keys (2 mm round, 3.5 mm tall) stand 16 mm either side of centre on the right-hand wall, and a small gold square marks the frame's near right corner. Shut over the frame: a steel shield, a frame 54 by 47 mm and 1.2 mm thick with a 44 by 35 mm window, hinged along its far edge (it opens up to 120 degrees), with a tongue and a lip 8 mm tall on its near end. Down along the frame's right side, over the shield's right edge: the socket lever, a 3 mm steel rod 108 mm long that pivots at its near end (it opens up to 135 degrees), with a 12 mm handle bent to the right at its far end carrying a black knob 8 mm across; a gold catch (4 mm round, 8 mm long) on a spring stands over the rod 22 mm from the handle and holds the lever down. The processor: a green substrate 45 by 37.5 mm and 1.2 mm thick with two notches (2.5 mm wide, 2 mm deep) in one long edge and a gold triangle in the corner next to them, under a steel lid 30 by 30 mm and 3.2 mm thick; 30 g. It lies on a black stand 3 by 3 cm and 1 cm tall at x 25, y -21.5, turned a quarter turn from the socket, its notches facing away from the arms.
scoring: The processor is seated when its lowest point is within 0.5 mm of the board, it is flat within 1 degree, its centre is within 0.8 mm of the pocket's, it is turned within 2 degrees of the socket's orientation (notches on the keys) and it is still (under 1 cm/s). Not seated, anywhere: 0. Seated: 0.4. Seated with the shield shut (within 3 degrees): 0.7. Seated, the shield shut and the lever down under its catch (within 2 degrees; a lever laid on top of the catch sits at about 4): 1.0, held for 1 s. A processor turned the wrong way rides on the keys and is not seated. Possible scores: 0, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0. To check a real trial: a top photo for the lid square in the frame and the lever under its tab, and a side view for the processor flat.
reset_notes: Shut the shield, put the lever down under its catch, and put the processor back on its stand, turned a quarter turn from the socket with its notches facing away from the arms.
fidelity: The socket has no contacts: its floor is flat. The lever is a rigid rod and its catch a sprung pin that moves aside (a real lever's wire flexes out from under a fixed tab), so the lever snaps under it and pulls out. The handle carries an 8 mm knob to grip. The shield closes on its hinge alone and doesn't clamp the substrate. The frame's inner edges and the keys are rounded as lead-ins. Lid size, thicknesses and the 30 g mass are approximate.
